hook: Childers moved from Fortune 20 operations, Amazon's peak IT infrastructure and GE's global virtualization program, into the CIO seat at a precision aerospace manufacturer. His IoT initiative at Meyer Tool, measuring machine productivity and availability on the factory floor, is the kind of applied industrial AI that rarely makes headlines but represents the actual frontier of operational technology in advanced manufacturing.
name: Vern Childers

quote.text: As a change agent who creates a dynamic, responsive, and business-driven IT organization, he has led several groundbreaking initiatives for the company.

reading.body:
Vern Childers represents a career path that moves enterprise-scale infrastructure experience into precision manufacturing, where the real constraint on operational AI is not algorithms but machine-level data collection.

His progression from GE's global virtualization program to managing Amazon's peak IT infrastructure across three consecutive Q4 cycles gave him direct exposure to the two hardest problems in enterprise computing: consolidating physical infrastructure at scale, and keeping systems reliable under maximum load. Those problems are not abstract at Meyer Tool. An aerospace component manufacturer runs tightly scheduled machine time, and unplanned downtime carries certification and delivery consequences that software-only businesses do not face. The IoT program he launched tracks machine productivity, availability, and downtime, which means the data layer has to reach the factory floor before any higher analysis is possible.

The data covers his career chronology and the scope of his current role, but it does not include specifics on the architecture of the IoT program, the number of machines instrumented, the data volumes involved, or how outputs connect to broader manufacturing execution or enterprise systems. It also does not address compute infrastructure at Meyer Tool. What the record does establish is that industrial AI at this level begins with instrumentation, and that the people building it tend to come from operations backgrounds rather than research ones.
